newsitem.title: THAILAND: Thai stocks tumble to near 8-year low as baht battered.
newsitem.headline: Thai stocks tumble to near 8-year low as baht battered.

text.p: Thai stocks were hammered on Wednesday amid renewed concerns over stuttering economic growth and a fresh market attack on the baht.
The composite SET Index lost 5.28 percent shortly after the market reopened in the afternoon. It fell 31.67 points to stay near its eight year low of 568.57 on moderate 3.83 billion baht turnover.
The baht attacks and forced selling of leveraged stocks held by retail investors aggravated the market's slide, they said.
"Stock selling is across the board. Most selling orders are from foreign investors," said a broker at Nava Finance and Securities.
"The baht is the main reason for the free fall today," said another trader at a major U.S. brokerage.
"Somehow, the investors were not convinced that the government can let the interest rate come down without having to adjust the currency system," the trader said.

Concerns over the health of the Thai economy, a slump in the stock market and speculation over a possible change in the Thai finance portfolio combined to batter the baht, driving it to 26.250-26.300 to the dollar on Wednesday morning, dealers said.
Currency dealers dumped the baht for the dollar despite assurances from the Bank of Thailand that it had no plan to change its baht fixing policy.
The Bank of Thailand later said it and the Monetary Authority of Singapore had jointly intervened in the foreign exchange market to defend the baht.
The central bank said its action was "aimed at stemming excessive speculative activities which may lead to disorderly conditions in the Thai and regional financial markets".
It said other appropriate measures will be taken as necessary.
The central bank intervention helped the currency recover to 26.050-26.100 by late afternoon.

Weak exports, poor first quarter results, beleaguered property and finance sectors, and uncertainty over the scope of the government's efforts to improve the situation have all been blamed for the stock market's recent falls.
The overall bearish economic outlook and continued rumours that Finance Minister Amnuay Viravan might be sacked also dampened sentiment, they said.
Prime Minister Chavalit Yongchaiyudh on Tuesday said Amnuay was staying in his position, and reaffirmed his six-month old government was doing all it could to help the economy.
"We have had high economic growth for the past 10 years so there must be some overheating and adjustment," Chavalit said after the weekly cabinet meeting.
Private economists predict the Thai economy will grow about five percent this year -- a sharp difference from the average nine percent growth the country enjoyed over the past decade.
